review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. The only way to get past this is to go and edit your save game (you guessed it, an XML file) in order to make it possible to complete some missions (this fix doesn't always work btw). This becomes a huge problem close to the end of the story. Without spoiling anything, you end up having two missions to do, and it seems that it doesn't matter the order you do them in, but if you choose wrong a subsequent mission will be skipped entirely (it is one of the most notorious bugs of the game) and you will miss part of the narrative and context. Seriously, if you are thinking of buying this game, in order to enjoy the story as it was meant to be played, you should first look up what I have just told you and figure out which mission you should do first when you get to that juncture, or be prepared to restart the whole game if you mess up (unbelievable).
5)The least the author could've done was to include a save management system, but of course, there is none. If you want to make sure you don't have to restart the game in case something gets screwed up (see above) you must manually backup your savegame file, and you have to be careful too...because although the game doesn't autosave normally it will autosave in certain circumstances, barely warning you that this has been done.
6)Although the game never crashes, there are a few technical bugs that wouldn't even be a problem if not for everything that i mentioned above. When working with the terminal, using the arrow keys to edit a command sometimes doesn't work properly, and there are a few other such things (sometimes, for example, you have to hack a computer twice because although you were able to hack in the first time, the game doesn't register it). There are also a few grammar mistakes that again, not really important on its own but if added to all of the above, it's just the "cherry" on top that you don't want...especially from a paid game, however cheap it is. 
7) There is a ranking system, but it doesn't work. No matter how many missions you complete and how high your rank is according to the success emails you get at the end of each completed mission, you are still the last on the list, with 0 points. It's annoying. Suggestion to the author: if a feature is too hard/you are to lazy to implement...don't include it, especially if it has no bearing on the gameplay whatsoever. It is pretty disappointing to reach the end of the game and see that in the eyes of your hacking faction you are still a newb. 

Now....I get it, it's an indie game...what did I expect? Well I expected something a little more functional. As a software developer myself I understand a few of the choices the author made, but sill...there are some laps in basic human logic that are beyond me. For example, it is obvious that is technically more difficult to write an "open world" style game as opposed to a linear game play experience. That's why the player is allowed to play one mission at a time. I really get it. What I don't get is if a linear game is what you wanted to code...THEN DO NOT OFFER CHOICES TO THE PLAYER THAT YOUR GAME IS UNABLE TO SUPPORT AND FORCE HIM/HER/THEY TO START OVER!!!
I also understand that is hard to test a piece of software by yourself, I have done it as my main occupation for many years. A few bugs are bound to crop up...but hey...IN THE CREDITS THERE ARE MENTIONED A WHOLE SLEW OF TESTERS...what the heck did they test exactly? Seriously...I want to see what test cases they ran on this....

I would ask for a refund...but hey if didn't get my 60 bucks back from CD Projekt RED for Cyberprank 2077 I certainly won't ask the 5 bucks i spent on this (i got the DLC too). Go ahead, enjoy your Starbucks latte on me.  
According to the author, this game started out as a 48h game jam project and was later refined for 2 and a half years to become what's on steam now. 2/3 YEARS??!?!?! THIS IS WHAT YOU COME UP WITH? I think the best definition of this game is just that....a barely interesting project  hurriedly cobbled together  for a 48h game jam event.

tl;dr; Do yourself a favor and buy Uplink Elite, which is obviously what this game wanted to be and failed...miserably. I'd be willing to gift Uplink to the author as well so that he can see how a game like this SHOULD be made.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is the lone developer's pet project, and it saddens me to give it a negative rating. Honestly, though, I just didn't enjoy the game at all. It is extraordinarily repetitive, and after a while, it feels that you're doing nothing except waiting for hacking animations to finish. With only 2 exceptions, [i] every [/i] mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?"

I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes. 

As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion.

All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

review_text_raw:
[b]A HACKER GROUP SEARCHING THE TRUTH[/b]
[i]Hacknet[/i] was available for free in Humble Bundle for a short period, long time ago. It's one of those game that normally I wouldn't buy. The game is centered on group of hackers that receives some contracts from people that wants to obtain something: it could be retrieving a file or cancel something from another user computer. For the entire game, you will see the Hacknet OS, a system that allows to execute some tools and let you inside other networks and devices.

[h1]VERY REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY[/h1]
At the beginning [i]Hacknet[/i] seems promising. The game make you feel like you are a real hacker, trying to break in other people computers, but after a while everything repeat itself. You always do the same things: hack devices ports, with specific executables that you just need to download from the hacker group server, once you are in, you need to check the files, and once you completed the task, simply reply to the client request mail, with details needed. Some of these contract are challenging and it will take a lot of time, trying to understand which is the solution of the enigma. Usually there is not only one way to go, but you can complete the mission in different ways. The real problem is that missions are all the same and nothing really change for the whole game.

[h1]CANCEL THE LOGS[/h1]
One of the things that the game never stop to stress you out is deleting the logs in a computer after you finished to snoop around. At the beginning I did it, because I was scared that I could be traced, losing the mission. After a while, because you have so many steps to do in order to complete the contract, I forgot to clean them several times, and nothing happened. They cannot trace me so I simply stopped to worry about it: I canceled only when I remembered.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Hacknet[/i] could have potential. It looks different and interesting, but, as I've mentioned before, you need to do always the same bunch of actions, and this made me lose the interest in the game. I have still to complete the main story, but I think I played enough to express an opinion on this title. I really wanted to buy also DLCs, but after this experience, I think I stop here my experience with this game.

review_text_raw:
Got the game for free and it has been sitting in my backlog for a while. Some while ago I finally decided to clear this game with high expectations seeing it receive a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately I was faced with only disappointment.

At first the gameplay is intriguing and engaging. The terminal style UI certainly looks cool. There are quests that procedurally guide you through the mechanics of the game, and the discovery process keeps the gameplay fresh, but not for long until you join the hacker organization.

From that point what you do is just repeating the same hacking routine again and again, and it gets repetitive very quickly. At this point the only thing left that can do some good for this game is the story. My last hope for the game was that after hours of labour I would uncover traces of a big conspiracy that leads me to something like stopping a skynet, or fighting myself in a moral conflict, you get the meaning.

But no! The main plot is linear and doesn't have much depth to it. It was so uninspiring that I didn't even know I came to the end of the story, just after I did the usual hacking stuff I was greeted with a voice recording and I was like "is that it?".

Also the 'hacking experience' is far from realistic. But I guess it serves the point of letting people feel like they're a hacker.

I really want to like this game, but I couldn't. The music is good though, I think it's the only plus side.

TL;DR: Cool hacking-look UI, repetitive hacking routine, weak story

[h1]WARNING this review will have spoilers, however, I've already marked what I consider to be spoilers[/h1]

This review is [b]NOT[/b] for people who plan on going through this game and only doing what the scripts you to. This is for those who want to delete everything they can get into after downloading files that they'd like to save as trophies or blackmail.

This is a great game, I have yet to beat it but I've loved most of the time I've put into this game, which is why I'm sad to say that I can't recommend this game. My main issue with it is the fact that its dead, unless I'm mistaken which is very possible. This game is filled with hand placed text and files as well as scripted events. At one point in the game, towards the beginning, [spoiler]you have to hack into a clicker game (that you can actually play which is super cool!) in order to delete an elite player's save so that he can show off his clicker power once more! I deleted the entire game alongside EVERYONE's saves. If you choose to do this you don't need to fret, you can still play the game, which is the main issue... WHY CAN I PLAY A DELETED GAME?[/spoiler] This trend follows with pretty much any computer or server you hack into, no one reacts, nothing gets repaired over time and things still work... WHY? Why does no one care if I've deleted ALL their system files, why do things still work even after I've deleted the file that basically says "DO NOT DELETE OR WILL STOP WORKING!!!" And why can't I blackmail people? I probably won't be able to get myself to beat this game because it just feels dead to me, sure its a lot of fun, but the immersion is killed the second I try to jump ship and do my own thing.

A second issue some people may have with this game is that it expects you to know, or figure out, everything outside of the few basic things it teachs you from the start, sometimes while being put under the clock. I have no real gripes with this, the game doesn't hold your hand (which I like), the only reason I mentioned it was for those players who don't like being forced to figure out solutions they've never been taught.

tl;dr: This game is dead, do anything outside of the script and its like nothing happened and no one cares. Make sure you can think on your feet and make sure you don't mind finding solutions to problems you've never even seen before.

I have been waiting for the game to start, and now that I'm halfway through I've given up. It's boring and pointless. There is no story, there are no choices (even though the game wants you to think there are). That aside, it's not really a hacking game. "Hacking" just means typing the same commands and waiting for them to execute... every time... for every PC in the network.

Another big problem is that the game implies that it will use real world logic but then it doesn't. Like I can't execute a file on a PC I'm connected to? Since when? 

Instructions are never clear and even if they are I hate that the game forces me to only do things how the dev intended. Specifically for advcancing missions, it's never clear whether I just need to read the file or send it or send the password contained in it. All of those should work, not just one!

There are bugs - mostly soft locks, which is unacceptable for such a simple game.

Instead of spending time on the visualizations for each tool the dev should have spent time designing mechanics around them. For instance the firewall analyzer is okay. Not fun, but it's not completely idle, you have to do something. Each tool has to be like that, there has to be some mini-game associated with it, or there has to be some strategy as to which tools are used in what order.

I don't know what the music was like. It was so repeptitve so annoying I turned it off and played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines OST. 

The only thing I liked about the game is the environmental storytelling. The chat logs sound EXACTLY like the Old Internet days. Kudos to the author for the research!

You type commands(always the same few), wait a few seconds, skim through what you've gotta skim, turn the current assignment in, rinse and repeat.

Sadly, the game lacks any real player agency: You're just following a series of steps with minimal variation, with no real difficulty to speak of at any point, and no freedom, be it to approach things differently, or do something for your own reasons.

I'm frankly baffled at how so many people recommend it, it's essentially a nongame.
